claim: IFN-α pretreatments lead to opposite effects (priming versus desensitization) depending on input durations.
source: We found that IFN-α pretreatments lead to opposite effects, priming versus desensitization, depending on input durations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential responses to IFN pretreatments of different durations, as presented in the manuscript's results section.

claim: The opposite effects of IFN-α pretreatments are governed by a regulatory network composed of a fast-acting positive feedback loop and a delayed negative feedback loop mediated by upregulation of USP18.
source: These effects are governed by a regulatory network composed of a fast-acting positive feedback loop and a delayed negative feedback loop, mediated by upregulation of ubiquitin-specific peptidase 18 (USP18).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from USP18 knockdown experiments and computational modeling showing the roles of positive and negative feedback loops.

claim: USP18 upregulation can only be initiated at the G1/early S phases of cell cycle upon treatment onset.
source: We further revealed that USP18 upregulation can only be initiated at the G1/early S phases of cell cycle upon the treatment onset, resulting in heterogeneous and delayed induction kinetics in single cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cell cycle reporters (CDK2 activity reporter and FUCCI) and cell cycle synchronization experiments.

claim: Cell cycle gating provides temporal compartmentalization of feedback loops, enabling duration-dependent desensitization to repetitive stimulations.
source: This cell cycle gating provides a temporal compartmentalization of feedback loops, enabling duration-dependent desensitization to repetitive stimulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and computational modeling showing how cell cycle stages affect USP18 induction and subsequent cellular responses.

claim: A 2-hr or 10-hr IFN-α pretreatment accelerates and enhances the transcriptional response to a second IFN-α input.
source: We found that a 2- or 10-hr pretreatment accelerated and enhanced the transcriptional response to the second IFN-α input, as indicated by increased induction rates and levels of the PIRF9-driven reporter, compared to the control without pretreatment (Figure 1E and F; compare green and blue curves/bars with black ones).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F, measuring PIRF9-YFP reporter induction.

claim: A 24-hr IFN-α pretreatment dramatically decreases the transcriptional response to a second IFN-α input.
source: Intriguingly, a 24-hr pretreatment, however, dramatically decreased the transcriptional response to the second input (Figure 1E and F compare red curves/bars with black ones).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F, measuring PIRF9-YFP reporter induction.

claim: USP18 is required for desensitization induced by prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
source: These results indicate that USP18 is required for desensitization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that USP18 knockdown abolishes the desensitization effect of 24-hr pretreatment.

claim: A 24-hr IFN-α pretreatment substantially diminishes STAT1 nuclear translocation in WT cells upon a second IFN input.
source: We found that a 24-hr IFN-α pretreatment substantially diminished STAT1 nuclear translocation in WT cells upon the second IFN input, whereas 2-hr or 10-hr pretreatment shows a modest effect (Figure 2A, 'WT'; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A and B.

claim: The desensitization effect of 24-hr IFN-α pretreatment on STAT1 nuclear translocation is abolished when USP18 expression is knocked down.
source: However, this desensitization effect was abolished when USP18 expression was knocked down (Figure 2A, 'USP18-KD'; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, C and D.

claim: IFN-α pretreatments boost transcriptional responses in USP18-KD cells upon a second input, exhibiting priming effects independent of their durations or doses.
source: Furthermore, in accord with STAT1 nuclear translocation, IFN-α pretreatments boosted the transcriptional responses in USP18-KD cells upon the second input, exhibiting priming effects independent of their durations or doses (Figure 2, B and C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, B and C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, D–F.

claim: Knocking down SOCS1 does not affect the desensitization of STAT1 nuclear translocation by prolonged IFN pretreatment.
source: In contrast to USP18-KD, knocking down SOCS1 (SOCS1-KD) did not affect the desensitization of STAT1 nuclear translocation by the prolonged IFN pretreatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: IFN-α pretreatment results in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD (~15 times more effective than in WT).
source: We found that the IFN-α pretreatment resulted in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD, ~15 times more effective than in WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from viral replication assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
source: We found that the IFN-α pretreatment resulted in a much more dramatic repression of viral replication in USP18-KD, ~15 times more effective than in WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that USP18-mediated desensitization attenuates the antiviral effect of prolonged IFN-α pretreatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of viral replication between WT and USP18-KD cells with IFN-α pretreatment.

claim: The computational model suggests that a prolonged input is required to initiate USP18 upregulation.
source: In summary, our modeling results suggest that a prolonged input is required to initiate USP18 upregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that a delay in USP18 upregulation is necessary to reproduce experimental observations.

claim: The fitting error between model simulations and experimental data reaches the minimum when the delay time in USP18 upregulation is 8 hours.
source: By fitting the model to the data for each assigned delay time, we found that the fitting error (between simulations and data) reaches the minimum when the delay time is 8 hrs (Figure 3, B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling and fitting to experimental data, as shown in Figure 3, B and C.

claim: Repetitive transient IFN inputs shorter than the delay time lead to a higher transcriptional response than a prolonged input with the same total treatment time.
source: The model further predicted that repetitive transient IFN inputs that are shorter than the delay time could be less able to induce the USP18-mediated negative feedback loop and hence could lead to a higher transcriptional response than that induced by a prolonged input with the same total treatment time.
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: Pulsatile IFN inputs with 5 × 8-hr pulses produce a higher transcriptional response than a 40-hr sustained input.
source: This prediction was tested experimentally and a higher transcriptional response, indicated by the PIRF9-driven reporter, was observed when 5 × 8-hr IFN pulses were given, compared to that induced by a single 40-hr treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pulsatile versus sustained IFN inputs.

claim: The difference in transcriptional response between pulsatile and sustained IFN inputs is abolished in USP18-KD cells.
source: Furthermore, this difference caused by different input dynamics was abolished in USP18-KD cells (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: IRF9 and USP18, although induced by the same upstream JAK-STAT signaling, exhibit strikingly different activation times.
source: We found that, consistent with our model, IRF9 and USP18, although induced by the same upstream JAK-STAT signaling, exhibited strikingly different activation times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the dual reporter cell line tracking IRF9 and USP18 expression.

claim: PIRF9-driven expression is induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells.
source: PIRF9-driven expression was induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells; in contrast, PUSP18-driven expression exhibited a slow and heterogeneous kinetics (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PUSP18-driven expression exhibits a slow and heterogeneous kinetics.
source: PIRF9-driven expression was induced with a fast and relatively uniform kinetics among cells; in contrast, PUSP18-driven expression exhibited a slow and heterogeneous kinetics (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: About 83.3% of cells show modest delays in USP18 induction (<10 hrs), whereas 16.7% of cells exhibit more prolonged delays (>10 hrs).
source: Intriguingly, we quantified the delay times of UPS18 induction, relative to that of IRF9, in single cells and observed a long-tail distribution: about 83.3% of cells showed modest delays in induction (<10 hrs), whereas the other 16.7% cells exhibited more prolonged delays (>10 hrs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantifying delay times in single cells.

claim: The mean activation times of IRF9 and USP18 are 7.9008 ± 0.1914 and 12.1620 ± 0.2349 hrs, respectively.
source: The mean activation times (with 95% confidence interval) of IRF9 and USP18 are 7.9008 ± 0.1914 and 12.1620 ± 0.2349 hrs, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells show modest delays in USP18 induction if IFN treatment is added at the early phase of their cell cycles (0–35% of the cell cycle).
source: We found that cells showed modest delays if the treatment was added at the early phase of their cell cycles (0–35% of the cell cycle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing the relationship between cell cycle stage and USP18 delay time.

claim: In cells that progressed beyond the early phase of cell cycle, IFN treatment cannot initiate USP18 induction until the next cell cycle, resulting in extended delay times.
source: In contrast, in those cells that progressed beyond this phase, the IFN treatment could not initiate USP18 induction until the next cell cycle, resulting in extended delay times proportional to the times needed to reach the next cell cycle (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cell-to-cell variability in USP18 delay times stems from different cell cycle stages among cells at the treatment onset.
source: These results suggest that the cell-to-cell variability in USP18 delay times may stem from different cell cycle stages among cells at the treatment onset.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the relationship between cell cycle stage and USP18 delay time.

claim: Cell cycle synchronization substantially reduces the fraction of cells with prolonged delays of USP18 induction.
source: As expected, we observed that cell cycle synchronization substantially reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delays of USP18 induction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cell cycle synchronization methods shown in Figure 5A.

claim: G1 and S cells show relatively fast USP18 activation times, whereas a large fraction of G2 cells exhibit a substantial delay in USP18 induction.
source: We found that G1 and S cells showed relatively fast USP18 activation times, whereas a large fraction of G2 cells exhibited a substantial delay in USP18 induction (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the CDK2 activity reporter shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The G1/S stages allow rapid induction of USP18 expression, but the G2 stage restrains the initiation of gene induction, resulting in a prolonged delay in USP18 expression.
source: These results, together with the cell cycle inhibitor data in Figure 5A, confirmed the influence of cell cycle stages on USP18 induction. The G1/S stages allow rapid induction of expression induction, but the G2 stage restrains the initiation of gene induction, resulting in a prolonged delay in USP18 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell cycle reporter and synchronization experiments.

claim: The promoter of USP18 contains a large number of CpG sites, which are highly methylated in all cell types examined.
source: Intriguingly, the promoter of USP18 contains a large number of CpG sites, which are highly methylated in all the cell types examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation profiles.

claim: The IRF9 promoter contains less CpG sites and is less methylated than the USP18 promoter.
source: In contrast, the IRF9 promoter contains less CpG sites and is less methylated (Komaki, 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation profiles and citation to previous work.

claim: Decitabine treatment reduces the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction.
source: We observed that the decitabine treatment reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction, which is in part due to earlier USP18 upregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), supporting that the promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using decitabine treatment shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction.
source: We observed that the decitabine treatment reduced the fraction of cells with prolonged delay times in USP18 induction, which is in part due to earlier USP18 upregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), supporting that the promoter methylation inhibits USP18 induction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that decitabine (a DNA methyltransferase inhibitor) reduces USP18 induction delay.

claim: Cell cycle stages impact the initiation of USP18 upregulation through modulating the promoter methylation level.
source: In summary, our results suggested that the cell cycle stages may impact the initiation of USP18 upregulation through modulating the promoter methylation level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing the effects of cell cycle stages and DNA methylation on USP18 induction.

claim: The open window length for immediate USP18 induction is estimated to be 7.3 hrs (~33% of 21.82 hrs cell cycle length).
source: The model was fit to the experimentally-determined distribution of USP18 delay times within a cell cycle (Figure 6B; the data from Figure 4E) and we obtained an estimate of the open window length to be 7.3 hrs (~33% of 21.82 hrs).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling fitted to experimental data.

claim: The 24-hr pretreatment effectively induces USP18 upregulation to a much higher extent than 2-hr and 10-hr pretreatments.
source: We observed that the 24-hr pretreatment effectively induced UPS18 upregulation, to a much higher extent than those upon 2-hr and 10-hr pretreatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by stochastic simulations of the computational model.

claim: Higher levels of USP18 expression by prolonged pretreatment lead to reduced IRF9 induction upon the second stimulation at the single-cell level.
source: Importantly, as shown in Figure 6C, the higher levels of USP18 expression by the prolonged pretreatment lead to reduced IRF9 induction upon the second stimulation at the single-cell level, qualitatively in agreement with our experimental data (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by both computational modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines.
source: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines, which are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses to limit pathogen spread via reducing protein production, upregulating antiproliferative and antiviral genes, and programmed cell death (Schneider et al., 2014; Barber and defense, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Type I IFNs are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses.
source: IFN-α is a member of the type I IFN family of cytokines, which are synthesized and secreted in mammals upon pathogen infection and initiate innate immune responses to limit pathogen spread via reducing protein production, upregulating antiproliferative and antiviral genes, and programmed cell death (Schneider et al., 2014; Barber and defense, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IFN-α has been clinically used in treatments of hepatitis B and C infection, HIV infection, melanoma, kidney cancer, leukemia and lymphoma.
source: IFN-α has also been clinically used in treatments of a variety of diseases, such as hepatitis B and C infection, HIV infection, melanoma, kidney cancer, leukemia and lymphoma (Watanabe et al., 2013; Medrano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IFN-α exerts its anti-pathogenic and anti-proliferative effects by activating the JAK-STAT pathway, leading to the expression of over 300 IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: IFN-α exerts its anti-pathogenic and anti-proliferative effects by activating the Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway, leading to the expression of over 300 IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) (Schneider et al., 2014; Schoggins and Rice, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IFN-α binds to IFNAR, triggering the activation of JAK1 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2.
source: IFN-α binds to a heterodimeric transmembrane receptor, the IFN-α receptor (IFNAR), triggering the activation of receptor-associated kinases Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), which in turn phosphorylate transcription factors signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) and STAT2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge of the IFN-α signaling pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2 dimerize and associate with IRF9 to form ISGF3 complex.
source: The phosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2 dimerize and associate with IFN-regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) to form IFN-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3) complex.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge of the IFN-α signaling pathway.

claim: ISGF3 translocates to the nucleus and binds to ISRE, activating the transcription of ISGs.
source: ISGF3 then translocates to the nucleus and binds to the DNA consensus sequences, known as IFN-stimulated response element (ISRE), activating the transcription of ISGs (Platanias, 2005; Schreiber, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread.
source: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread, whereas a response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis (Choubey and Moudgil, 2011; Crow, 2016; McNab et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis.
source: A response that is too short or too weak will fail to limit pathogen spread, whereas a response that is too prolonged or too strong will result in tissue damage, organ failure, and carcinogenesis (Choubey and Moudgil, 2011; Crow, 2016; McNab et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In some studies, prior exposure to IFN-α accelerates cells' responses to the second IFN input, enabling a 'priming' effect.
source: In some studies, a prior exposure to IFN-α accelerates cells' responses to the second IFN input, enabling a 'priming' effect (Abreu et al., 1979; Kuri et al., 2009; Rodriguez-Pla et al., 2014; Phipps-Yonas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In other studies, pretreatment with IFN-α diminishes the responses to the following stimulation, resulting in a 'desensitization' effect.
source: In other studies, however, a pretreatment with IFN-α diminishes the responses to the following stimulation, resulting in a 'desensitization' effect (Scagnolari and Antonelli, 2018; Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009; Makowska et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex that mediates IFN-driven gene expression (Cheon et al., 2013), and IFN-induced chromatin modifications (Kamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFN-induced chromatin modifications contribute to the priming effect.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the priming effect can be attributed to the expression induction of IRF9, STAT1 and STAT2, which are components of ISGF3 transcriptional complex that mediates IFN-driven gene expression (Cheon et al., 2013), and IFN-induced chromatin modifications (Kamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: USP18 is a major negative regulator of JAK-STAT signaling.
source: To determine the mechanism of desensitization caused by the prolonged pretreatment, we use a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down the expression of ubiquitin-specific peptidase 18 (USP18), a major negative regulator of JAK-STAT signaling that we identified previously (Zou et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008; Ritchie et al., 2004; Malakhova et al., 2003), in the reporter cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, USP18-KD).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: USP18 is transcriptionally upregulated by IFN treatment and exerts inhibition of IFN-α signaling at the receptor level, forming a negative feedback loop.
source: USP18 is transcriptionally upregulated by IFN treatment and exerts inhibition of IFN-α signaling at the receptor level, forming a negative feedback loop (Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009; François-Newton et al., 2011; Arimoto et al., 2017; Malakhova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Individual cells respond to IFNs in a highly heterogeneous manner, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recent studies found that individual cells respond to IFNs in a highly heterogeneous manner, both in vitro (Czerkies et al., 2018; Rand et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2015) and in vivo (Miao et al., 2010; Stifter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Traditional assays that measure averaged responses across populations at static time points may not accurately characterize cells' responses to IFNs.
source: Therefore, traditional assays that measure averaged responses across populations at static time points may not be able to accurately characterize cells' responses to IFNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of heterogeneous single-cell responses.

claim: A rapid nuclear translocation of STAT1 (within ~0.5 hr) is observed in response to IFN-α stimulation.
source: We observed a rapid nuclear translocation (within ~0.5 hr) of STAT1 followed by a gradual increase in PIRF9-driven gene expression in response to IFN-α stimulation (Figure 1B and C; Video 1), consistent with traditional western blotting results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: STAT1 nuclear translocation correlates temporally with the increase in PIRF9-driven transcriptional activity.
source: STAT1 nuclear translocation correlated temporally with the increase in PIRF9-driven transcriptional activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A dose higher than 10 ng/ml IFN-α is required for desensitization in 24-hr pretreatment.
source: We also examined how changing the dose of IFN pretreatment impacts the effect on the response to the second input and found that a dose higher than 10 ng/ml is required for desensitization in 24-hr pretreatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, A–C.

claim: The effect of desensitization decreases as a function of break time between pretreatment and second stimulation.
source: Furthermore, we tested how the break time between pretreatment and second stimulation influences desensitization and found that the effect of desensitization decreased as a function of break time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: IRF9 is one of the major early response ISGs and encodes a key component of the ISGF3 complex.
source: We chose IRF9 because it has been well defined as one of the major early response ISGs and it encodes a key component of the ISGF3 complex (Cheon et al., 2013; Tsuno et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 100 ng/ml (10,000 IU/ml) IFN-α is a sub-saturating and clinically relevant concentration.
source: We examined single-cell responses to various doses of IFN-α (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and chose 100 ng/ml (10,000 IU/ml), a sub-saturating and clinically relevant (Tarhini et al., 2012) concentration, for the following analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and experimental dose-response data.

claim: The heterogeneity in upstream components (STAT1 and IRF9) contributes partially to cell-to-cell variation in the expression levels of USP18.
source: To determine the source of clonal heterogeneity in USP18 induction, we analyzed the relationship of USP18 expression with STAT1 or IRF9 expression at the single-cell level and found that the heterogeneity in these upstream components contributed partially to cell-to-cell variation in the expression levels of USP18.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing correlations between USP18 and upstream components.

claim: The delay times of USP18 upregulation correlate poorly with STAT1 or IRF9 expression.
source: However, the delay times of USP18 upregulation correlated poorly with STAT1 or IRF9 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell cycle progression is a major factor that coordinates gene expression.
source: We further considered the contribution of the cell cycle stage at IFN treatment onset, as the cell cycle progression has been shown as a major factor that coordinates gene expression (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Serum starvation arrests cells in G1 stage.
source: Specifically, we treated cells with serum starvation (Langan and Chou, 2011), lovastatin (Keyomarsi et al., 1991; Javanmoghadam-Kamrani and Keyomarsi, 2008), and roscovitine (Kolodziej et al., 2015), all of which arrested cells in G1 or G1/S stage, prior to the IFN-α treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lovastatin arrests cells in G1 or G1/S stage.
source: Specifically, we treated cells with serum starvation (Langan and Chou, 2011), lovastatin (Keyomarsi et al., 1991; Javanmoghadam-Kamrani and Keyomarsi, 2008), and roscovitine (Kolodziej et al., 2015), all of which arrested cells in G1 or G1/S stage, prior to the IFN-α treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Roscovitine arrests cells in G1 or G1/S stage.
source: Specifically, we treated cells with serum starvation (Langan and Chou, 2011), lovastatin (Keyomarsi et al., 1991; Javanmoghadam-Kamrani and Keyomarsi, 2008), and roscovitine (Kolodziej et al., 2015), all of which arrested cells in G1 or G1/S stage, prior to the IFN-α treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DNA methylation decreases in G1 and increases during S and G2 phases.
source: Previous studies revealed global variations of epigenetic modifications during cell cycle. For instance, DNA methylation decreases in G1 and increases during S and G2 phases (Brown et al., 2007; Woodcock et al., 1986; Desjobert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreased promoter methylation leads to increased USP18 expression in breast cancer.
source: This result is consistent with a previous study showing that a decreased promoter methylation leads to increased USP18 expression in breast cancer (Tan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Decitabine leads to cell cycle arrest in G1 or G2.
source: We note that decitabine also leads to cell cycle arrest in G1 or G2 (Shin et al., 2013; Lavelle et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only a small fraction of decitabine-treated cells is arrested in G1.
source: Because only a small fraction of decitabine-treated cells is arrested in G1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) and USP18 induction is largely delayed in G2 (Figure 5C), the accelerating effect of decitabine on USP18 expression should be via inhibition of methylation rather than cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The accelerating effect of decitabine on USP18 expression is via inhibition of methylation rather than cell cycle arrest.
source: Because only a small fraction of decitabine-treated cells is arrested in G1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) and USP18 induction is largely delayed in G2 (Figure 5C), the accelerating effect of decitabine on USP18 expression should be via inhibition of methylation rather than cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data comparing cell cycle arrest patterns and USP18 induction kinetics.

claim: The length of a full cell cycle was estimated to be 21.82 hrs based on single-cell time trace measurements.
source: The length of a full cell cycle was estimated to be 21.82 hrs based on the single-cell time trace measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the duration of pretreatment is shorter than or close to the delay time (e.g. 2- or 10-hr pretreatment), USP18 can only be partially induced in some cells so that the fast-acting positive feedback loop and the priming effect dominate.
source: When the duration of pretreatment is shorter than or close to the delay time (e.g. 2- or 10-hr pretreatment), USP18 can only be partially induced in some cells so that the fast-acting positive feedback loop and the priming effect dominate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental and modeling results.

claim: The 24-hr pretreatment can fully induce USP18-mediated negative feedback in most cells regardless of their cell cycle stages at treatment onset, resulting in desensitization to subsequent stimulation.
source: In contrast, the 24-hr pretreatment, longer than the entire length of a cell cycle, can fully induce USP18-mediated negative feedback in most cells regardless of their cell cycle stages at treatment onset, resulting in desensitization to subsequent stimulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental and modeling results.

claim: Key regulatory processes can be compartmentalized temporally by the cell cycle to decode dynamically varying signals.
source: In this way, key regulatory processes can be compartmentalized temporally by the cell cycle to decode dynamically varying signals.
evidence: This claim is a general conclusion inferred from the study's findings.

claim: Regulatory circuits with coupled negative and positive feedback loops can give rise to various dynamic behaviors, such as sustained oscillations and excitable gene expression.
source: Regulatory circuits with coupled negative and positive feedback loops have been discovered in many biological processes, and, depending on the specific mechanisms and kinetics, can give rise to various dynamic behaviors, such as sustained oscillations (Danino et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2017) and excitable gene expression (Ori et al., 2018; Süel et al., 2006; Mönke et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The coupled feedback system in the JAK-STAT pathway serves as a timer that measures the initial input duration and coordinates the temporal order of regulatory processes with opposing effects.
source: In this study, the coupled feedback system in the JAK-STAT pathway enables a new function of this well-studied network architecture: it serves as a timer that measures the initial input duration and coordinate the temporal order of regulatory processes with opposing effects, leading to differential cellular responses to subsequent stimuli.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion inferred from the study's findings.

claim: Delays in the expression of key regulatory factors have been found important for ensuring proper execution of biological functions.
source: Delays in the expression of key regulatory factors have been widely observed in signal-dependent transcriptional responses and have been found important for ensuring proper execution of biological functions (Hoffmann et al., 2002; Covert et al., 2005; Lemmon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanisms underlying delays in gene expression include extensive nucleosome occupancy at the promoter regions and cascades in gene expression programs.
source: Mechanisms underlying these delays include extensive nucleosome occupancy at the promoter regions (Hansen and O'Shea, 2015; Sen et al., 2020) and cascades in gene expression programs (Killip et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gene regulatory networks with specific topologies can give rise to delayed gene expression, enabling filtering of transient inputs.
source: Gene regulatory networks with specific topologies can also give rise to delayed gene expression, enabling filtering of transient inputs (Shen-Orr et al., 2002; Mangan et al., 2003; Toettcher et al., 2013; Thurley et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.
